title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
A music generation AI system was trained on copyrighted songs scraped from the internet without permission. The system learned to reproduce sections of those songs when given targeted prompts, creating outputs that closely resembled works by major artists. This is a model trained on unlicensed material and deployed to generate content that could infringe the copyrights used in its training, a failure that could have been caught by auditing training data sources and testing generated outputs against the source material before release.

The companies operating these systems declined to disclose what material they trained on and claimed their use of copyrighted work was fair use. Multiple lawsuits were filed by record labels, independent artists, and music publishers seeking damages. Whether the training constituted infringement, whether the generated outputs infringe existing copyrights, and whether any settlement or licensing agreements change the legal status of these systems are not established by the reporting.

summary:
Major record labels, including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, and others, have filed lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular AI music generators. The labels accuse these companies of scraping thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their AI models and then generating new music that directly reproduces sections of famous recordings. The lawsuits include a lengthy list of artists whose work was allegedly used, spanning from The Beatles and Frank Sinatra to modern acts like Blink-182 and Coldplay. The record labels submitted specific examples showing how targeted prompts can make the AI systems generate songs that closely resemble copyrighted material.

To build their case, the record labels demonstrated the problem by using specific prompts describing musical styles and artists, then comparing the AI-generated outputs to original songs they own the rights to. For instance, prompts referencing Chuck Berry's style allegedly produced 29 different outputs mimicking "Johnny B. Goode," and a Mariah Carey-themed prompt created a near-identical version of "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The two companies have refused to disclose their training data, claiming their use of copyrighted material constitutes fair use. Udio and Suno are headquartered in New York and Massachusetts respectively, where the separate lawsuits were filed.
